                                     PROJECT NO. 58000
   RULEMAKING TO UPDATE WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL TRANSMISSION
               COST RECOVERY IN THE ERCOT REGION
         BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS

                         COMMENTS OF SOREN M. WHITE, MD

I. INTEREST OF THE COMMENTER AND DISCLOSURES
Soren M. White, MD, submits these comments individually. He is the founder of GridSignals AI,
Inc., a research-stage company that develops reproducible ERCOT data and evaluation methods.
GridSignals does not currently sell coincident-peak curtailment services or transmission-cost-
avoidance services.
No client commissioned or funded these comments.
These comments present a bounded historical benchmark constructed from public ERCOT
forecast and Native Load data, supplemented by publicly available reporting concerning
historical four-coincident-peak determinations, and recommend further development of the
evidentiary record. The source limitations are set out in Appendix A. The commenter takes no
position on whether the Commission should adopt a twelve-coincident-peak methodology.
The provenance of that benchmark, including the date its parameterization was frozen and a
disclosure of the commenter’s prior exposure to certain 2026 information, is set out in Appendix
A.

II. COMMENTS ON PROPOSED §25.192

A. A simple public-data rule reduced the historical four-coincident-peak target to a finite
candidate set, in sample.
Using ERCOT forecast and Native Load inputs available by 9:00 a.m. Central Prevailing Time
on the operating day, together with the prior-year reference values described in Appendix A, a
deterministic rule evaluated over the 2023 through 2025 summer seasons designated
approximately 450 candidate hours across the three-summer calibration period, or approximately
150 hours per summer. Those called hours contained all twelve summer coincident-peak
reference intervals for that period. Each fell within hours ending 17 or 18, verified interval by
interval rather than by date alone. The specification, conventions, and known limitations appear
in Appendix A.
The result is stated narrowly because its limits matter as much as its content. The benchmark
does not establish:
   •   that any customer curtailed load during any candidate hour;
   •   that any customer’s metered demand was reduced or eliminated during any coincident-
       peak interval;
   •   that any customer avoided any transmission charge;
   •   that the rule would perform comparably outside its calibration period; or


                                                 1
    •     that approximately 150 called hours per summer is an acceptable operational burden.
         That depends on load size, opportunity cost, contractual obligations, and whether a call
         requires full or partial reduction. No such estimate is offered here.
What the benchmark does support is narrower and, for this proceeding, more useful. On the
disclosed reference set, the present four-interval methodology was historically reducible to a
finite, reproducible candidate set derived from public information and simple arithmetic. The
Commission should therefore not assume that changing the number or duration of coincident-
peak intervals will by itself eliminate coincident-peak forecasting and strategic load response.
Whether it does so is an empirical question about the structure of monthly peaks, and it can be
answered before adoption rather than discovered after.

B. The benchmark also illustrates what the public record cannot establish.
Public ERCOT data is sufficient to reconstruct the forecast available at the decision time and the
operational system-demand series. Reconstructing the settlement interval ultimately used
requires the authoritative coincident-peak calculation and the adjustments applied to it, including
the treatment of wholesale storage load. Public data is not sufficient to establish what occurred
behind a particular meter, what a customer had committed to do, who held authority to cause that
response, or whether the response satisfied an obligation.
That asymmetry bears directly on this proceeding. The proposed methodology assigns cost
responsibility using measured coincident demand, while the behavior producing that
measurement is governed by contracts, control systems, and operating arrangements outside the
public record. Comments in this docket, including these, are constrained by that limit. So is the
Commission’s ability to evaluate the proposal’s effects without directing the production of
additional data.

C. Measurement basis: implementation of the wholesale storage load exclusion.
The proposal excludes wholesale storage load from both DSP 12CP load and ERCOT 12CP
load, defining that term by reference to §25.501(m)(2). The exclusion is clear as drafted. Its
implementation is not.
The Commission should require ERCOT to:
   1.   identify, by report and field, the settlement-quality load series and the specific protocol
        calculation that will implement the exclusion;
   2.   clarify the treatment of energy storage charging load that falls outside the defined
        wholesale storage load category; and
   3.   publish interval data and workpapers sufficient for distribution service providers and
        affected customer classes to reproduce the resulting twelve-coincident-peak
        determinations independently.
A coincident-peak methodology allocates cost by identifying specific intervals. If reasonable
parties cannot reproduce which intervals were selected, the resulting allocation cannot be audited
by anyone other than the entity that performed it.
This is not a hypothetical concern, and ERCOT has already identified it. In Market Notice M-
B080124-01, ERCOT advised market participants that Real-Time operational Load includes
Wholesale Storage Load while the settlement four-coincident-peak determination excludes it
under Nodal Protocol Section 9.17.1, and advised participants to incorporate the Energy Storage

                                                  2
 Resource charging component if they wished operational monitoring to align with the settlement
calculation. Two series that track each other closely in magnitude can therefore identify different
intervals. A methodology whose selected intervals may affect a twenty-year large-load
minimum-billing obligation should not leave the governing load series to inference.

III. COMMENTS ON PROPOSED §25.193

A. The minimum billing demand, not the number of coincident-peak intervals, is the operative
constraint on coincident-peak forecasting.
For large load customers served by investor-owned distribution service providers, proposed
§§25.193(d) and 25.252(e), read together, establish a minimum billing demand equal to the
greater of contracted peak demand, the highest non-coincident peak demand in the preceding
year, or twelve-coincident-peak demand, with billing beginning with the first billing cycle after
transmission capacity is made available and continuing for 240 consecutive monthly payments
across the first twenty years.
Stated precisely: the proposed minimum billing demand cannot be reduced below the contracted-
peak or non-coincident-peak floor through coincident-peak forecasting alone. Other facts can
still change the billed amount, including contract amendment, capacity relinquishment, phased
energization, and changes in actual non-coincident peak demand. But the specific practice of
predicting and avoiding coincident-peak intervals does not reach the floor.
This is worth stating plainly because the move from four intervals to twelve is the more visible
feature of the proposal, while the floor is the provision doing the work.

B. The same provision that limits avoidance also limits the incentive to respond.
Once a large load customer’s twelve-coincident-peak demand falls to or below the greater of its
contracted peak demand and its rolling prior-year non-coincident peak, further coincident-peak
reduction no longer reduces its minimum billing demand. A formula that remains in force for
twenty years and is anchored to those measures therefore truncates, rather than eliminates, the
marginal billing incentive for peak response. To the extent the Commission values price-
responsive large load as a reliability resource, the design of that formula and the design of the
coincident-peak methodology are in tension. That tension is a reason to select the formula’s
parameters deliberately and on the record, rather than as an incidental consequence of the peak-
counting decision.

C. The record is not yet sufficient to choose among the alternatives the Commission has
identified.
The Commission has asked whether the minimum should vary by customer size or demand,
remain fixed for twenty years, phase down over time, employ a ratchet, employ a weighted
average, or use a lower measure. Each alternative distributes risk differently among the large
load, other customer classes, and the distribution service provider, and the magnitude of those
differences is an empirical question.
The commenter does not recommend a specific alternative, because the available public record
does not support a defensible choice among them. The Commission should instead direct Staff,
ERCOT, and affected distribution service providers to publish sensitivity workpapers
quantifying, under historical conditions, the billing and allocation consequences of at least a
fixed one-hundred-percent floor, a phased or ratcheted floor, a weighted-average floor, and terms

                                                 3
 shorter than twenty years. That record should be made before the Commission adopts a twenty-
year minimum-demand formula anchored to one hundred percent of contracted peak demand or
the rolling prior-year non-coincident peak.

IV. COMMENTS ON PROPOSED §25.252
Proposed §25.252(e)(1) requires billing to begin with the first billing cycle after transmission
capacity is made available. That provision is clear. Three implementation questions surrounding
it are not, and each is consequential enough to warrant express treatment in rule text rather than
being left to tariff, protocol, or contract.
   1.   Determination of availability. The rule should identify the standard for determining the
        date on which transmission capacity is made available, the entity responsible for that
        determination, the notice owed to the customer, and the treatment of partially available
        service.
   2.   Phased energization. Large loads frequently energize in stages over several years, and the
        proposal appears to treat contracted peak demand as a continuing floor. The rule should
        clarify whether contracted peak demand may be defined or amended by an approved
        phased-service schedule and, if so, what documentation, milestones, and effective dates
        govern each phase.
   3.   Capacity relinquishment. The rule should state the effect of relinquishing contracted
        capacity on the minimum billing demand and on the remaining term, and whether that
        capacity becomes available for reallocation under the applicable interconnection process.
Each of these determines the size or duration of an obligation that may run for twenty years and
240 billing cycles. Leaving them to later interpretation invites disputes that express drafting can
prevent.

V. REQUEST FOR DEVELOPMENT OF THE RECORD
The most useful step the Commission can take before adopting a twelve-interval methodology is
to require that the proposed design be tested against historical data and that the results be
published.
The commenter respectfully requests that the Commission direct ERCOT to prepare and publish
a historical backcast of the proposed methodology covering the five annual periods ending
September 30, 2021 through September 30, 2025, that is, October 1, 2020 through September 30,
2025, matching the annual period the proposal itself uses. The backcast should include:
   1.   the twelve monthly thirty-minute coincident-peak intervals that would have been selected
        in each annual period under the proposed definitions;
   2.   for each month, the selected interval and the next five highest thirty-minute intervals,
        with the megawatt margins separating them, so the Commission can evaluate how
        concentrated, closely contested, and susceptible to displacement the selected intervals
        are;
   3.   a decision-time analysis using archived as-published forecast vintages, so the
        Commission can distinguish how concentrated the monthly peaks were from how
        foreseeable they were to a party acting in advance;



                                                 4
    4.   the exact settlement-quality series and averaging method used, identified by report and
        field;
   5.   results computed both with and without the proposed wholesale storage load exclusion,
        so the effect of the exclusion is visible;
   6.   distribution service provider and customer class allocation workpapers showing how the
        resulting determinations translate into allocated cost;
   7.   minimum billing demand sensitivities as described in Section III.C; and
   8.   all of the above in machine-readable form sufficient for independent replication.
The interval-selection analysis can be performed from data ERCOT already holds. The allocation
workpapers and minimum-demand sensitivities may require additional tariff, customer-class,
contracted-demand, or billing inputs, and the Commission should direct Staff and affected
distribution service providers to supply them.
These are not open-ended research requests. Each item answers a question the Commission must
otherwise resolve by assumption: how concentrated monthly peaks are compared with summer
peaks; how close the competing intervals are; whether a selected interval is stable against
responsive load; and how allocated cost shifts among classes under actual historical conditions.

VI. CONCLUSION
The commenter takes no position on whether the Commission should adopt a twelve-coincident-
peak methodology. The bounded evidence presented here supports one proposition: on the
disclosed historical reference set, the current four-interval methodology was reducible to a finite
public-data candidate set, in sample, which is a reason to test rather than assume how an
alternative design will behave. Before adoption, the Commission should require a reproducible
historical backcast, candidate-interval margins, an identified measurement basis and storage-
exclusion implementation, and minimum billing demand sensitivities.

Respectfully submitted,

/s/ Soren M. White, MD
Soren M. White, MD
30 East 60th Street, Suite 2201
New York, New York 10022
212-396-3688

 APPENDIX A: BENCHMARK SPECIFICATION AND PROVENANCE

A.1 Decision rule
For each operating day d in a summer month m, the rule designates day d as a candidate day if:
                               Fd ≥ 0.9875 × max( Md , 0.95 × Pm, y−1 )
where:
Fd = the maximum forecast SystemTotal value among the hours ending 16, 17, and 18 on
operating day d, from the in-use model (InUseFlag = Y) in ERCOT report NP3-565-CD, Seven-
Day Load Forecast by Model and Weather Zone, taken from the latest as-published vintage with
a postDatetime at or before 9:00 a.m. Central Prevailing Time on operating day d. Forecast
revisions published after that cutoff are excluded.
Md = the highest daily peak of ERCOT Native Load hourly SystemTotal observed from the first
day of month m through operating day d minus one, using a Central Prevailing Time operating-
day convention. Operating day d is excluded because its afternoon peak has not occurred at the
decision cutoff.
Pm, y−1 = the same-month prior-year reference demand, drawn from the mixed-source reference set
described in A.5.
On a designated candidate day, the rule calls the hours ending 16, 17, and 18 Central Prevailing
Time.

A.2 Conventions
   •     Vintage selection: the latest as-published vintage with a postDatetime at or before the
         9:00 a.m. cutoff on the operating day. On the historical coincident-peak days in the
         calibration sample this was generally the 8:30 a.m. vintage. Later revisions are excluded.
   •     Operating day and time convention: dates were assigned using the source’s Central-time
         timestamp. The calibration covered June 1 through September 30 only, and every
         calibration date fell within Central Daylight Time, UTC minus five hours, so no daylight
         saving transition occurred within an evaluated window.
   •     Tie handling: the condition is stated as greater than or equal to, so a value exactly at the
         threshold designates a candidate day.
   •     Missing data: the calibration implementation treated the absence of an eligible decision-
         time forecast as no call. No operating day in the calibration period lacked an eligible
         forecast, so this convention did not affect the reported result. An operational application
         would require a separately specified missing-data policy.

A.3 Calibration and parameter selection
The threshold was selected by exhaustive search over the values 0.9800 to 1.0000 in increments
of 0.0025. The rule was evaluated on operating days in the 2023, 2024, and 2025 summer
seasons. Construction of the prior-year same-month floor also required reference values for 2022
through 2024, so the evaluation period and the input period are not the same. The selection
criterion was to maximize the number of summer coincident-peak reference intervals in the
disclosed calibration set that fell within the called window; among rules achieving maximum
reference-set capture, to minimize total called hours; and to break any remaining tie toward the

                                                   6
 highest threshold value. The selected value is 0.9875, which called all twelve reference intervals
across approximately 450 called hours over the three-summer period.

A.4 Provenance
The final parameterization was frozen on July 3, 2026. The dispatch pinning the baseline was
issued July 2, 2026. The rule was evaluated on the 2023 through 2025 summer seasons, with
prior-year floor inputs drawn from 2022 through 2024. No 2026 data was used in the calibration
or parameter-selection calculation. The governing evaluation protocol separately discloses the
commenter’s prior exposure to certain other June 2026 information.
The rule was not frozen before the beginning of the 2026 summer season. It was frozen before
any July 2026 coincident-peak-plausible day was scored under it.

A.5 Reference data and interval validation
The reference observations used both for scoring and for the prior-year floor are not a single
homogeneous series. ERCOT Native Load files supply the 2022 through 2024 reference
magnitudes and operational monthly-peak dates, which are hourly values. Where corroboration
was available it came from ERCOT-published records of peak demand and from publicly
available reporting. Depending on the observation, those records corroborate the date, the
magnitude, or both. They are not four-coincident-peak settlement determinations. Because the
relevant NP9-83-M records were not retrieved, these observations are not characterized as
primary-sourced settlement determinations. The 2025 values are publicly reported settled fifteen-
minute intervals. ERCOT Native Load includes wholesale storage load; settlement-quality load
excludes it, per ERCOT Nodal Protocols Section 9.17.1 and ERCOT market notice M-B080124-
01. The two quantities agree closely in magnitude and can disagree on which day carries the
monthly peak.
Interval validation was performed rather than assumed. The calibration credits a capture when a
coincident-peak date falls within the called set, and does not itself test the interval. That test was
performed separately for all twelve observations: each reference interval or hourly reference
band falls within hours ending 17 or 18, and imposing the interval-window condition changed no
result. For the 2025 observations the reference timestamps are stored by interval start while the
cited sources describe the intervals by ending time, which accounts for an apparent fifteen-
minute offset. That convention does not resolve the separate June 2025 value discrepancy
between 77,453 MW and 77,490 MW, which is disclosed in Appendix B.

A.6 Limitations of the reference data
During preparation of these comments the commenter was unable to retrieve the relevant 2022
through 2024 files of ERCOT’s four-coincident-peak calculation product, EMIL NP9-83-M,
through the retrieval method used, and ERCOT’s historical four-coincident-peak page publishes
determinations only through 2020. That experience does not establish that the files are
unavailable through every ERCOT channel.
The four 2022 monthly values supply the four 2023 prior-year floors. This limitation is disclosed
rather than resolved, and it is pertinent to Section V: the difficulty of assembling an authoritative,
machine-readable coincident-peak record from public sources is precisely why the Commission
should require ERCOT to publish one.



                                                  7
 A.7 Reproducibility
The decision rule is deterministic arithmetic and uses no proprietary input and no fitted statistical
model. Historical replication is more involved. It requires retrieval and parsing of ERCOT’s
archived as-published NP3-565-CD forecast vintages, ERCOT Native Load files, and coincident-
peak determinations subject to the limitations described in A.6, together with the conventions
stated above. The reported result was reproduced from the reference values identified here.

                                  EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
                     Project No. 58000. Comments of Soren M. White, MD.
The commenter takes no position on whether the Commission should adopt a twelve-coincident-
peak methodology. He recommends the following, each followed by its factual basis.
   •   Direct ERCOT to publish a five-year historical backcast of the proposed methodology for
       the annual periods ending September 30, 2021 through September 30, 2025. On the
       disclosed reference set, a deterministic public-data rule evaluated on the 2023 through
       2025 summer seasons designated approximately 450 candidate hours and called all
       twelve reference intervals. That in-sample result does not establish customer curtailment,
       reduced metered demand, or avoided charges; it shows only that the current method was
       historically reducible to a finite candidate set, which is a reason to test rather than assume
       how twelve intervals would behave.
   •   Require the backcast to report, for each month, the selected interval and the next five
       highest thirty-minute intervals with the megawatt margins separating them, and to include
       a decision-time analysis using archived forecast vintages, so that concentration is
       distinguished from foreseeability.
   •   Require ERCOT to identify, by report and field, the settlement-quality load series and
       protocol calculation implementing the wholesale-storage exclusion, clarify the treatment
       of charging load outside that category, and report the historical backcast both with and
       without the exclusion so its effect is visible. ERCOT has advised that operational Load
       includes wholesale storage load while the settlement calculation excludes it; a coincident-
       peak allocation that cannot be reproduced cannot be audited.
   •   Require publication of distribution service provider and customer class allocation
       workpapers in machine-readable form sufficient for independent replication, and direct
       Staff and affected distribution service providers to supply any tariff, contracted-demand,
       or billing inputs ERCOT does not hold.
   •   Direct Staff, ERCOT, and affected distribution service providers to publish minimum
       billing demand sensitivity workpapers covering a fixed one-hundred-percent floor, a
       phased or ratcheted floor, a weighted-average floor, and terms shorter than twenty years,
       before adopting a twenty-year minimum-demand formula anchored to one hundred
       percent of contracted peak demand or the rolling prior-year non-coincident peak. For
       customers subject to those provisions, proposed sections 25.193(d) and 25.252(e), read
       together, make the minimum billing demand, not the number of intervals, the operative
       constraint: it cannot be reduced below the contracted-peak or non-coincident-peak floor
       by coincident-peak forecasting alone. The formula therefore truncates, rather than
       eliminates, the marginal billing incentive for peak response.
   •   Define in rule text when transmission capacity is made available, the required notice, the
       treatment of partial service and phased energization, and how capacity relinquishment
       affects the minimum billing demand and remaining term.

                         COMMENTS OF SOREN M. WHITE, MD

I. INTEREST OF THE COMMENTER AND DISCLOSURES
Soren M. White, MD, submits these comments individually. He is the founder of GridSignals AI,
Inc., a research-stage company that develops reproducible ERCOT data and evaluation methods.
GridSignals does not currently sell coincident-peak curtailment services or transmission-cost-
avoidance services.
No client commissioned or funded these comments.

These comments present a bounded historical benchmark constructed from public ERCOT
forecast and Native Load data, supplemented by publicly available reporting concerning
historical four-coincident-peak determinations, and recommend further development of the
evidentiary record. The source limitations are set out in Appendix A. The commenter takes no
position on whether the Commission should adopt a twelve-coincident-peak methodology.

The provenance of that benchmark, including the date its parameterization was frozen and a
disclosure of the commenter's prior exposure to certain 2026 information, is set out in Appendix
A.

II. COMMENTS ON PROPOSED §25.192

A. A simple public-data rule reduced the historical four-coincident-peak target to a Bnite
candidate set, in sample.
Using ERCOT forecast and Native Load inputs available by 9:00 a.m. Central Prevailing Time
on the operating day, together with the prior-year reference values described in Appendix A, a
deterministic rule evaluated over the 2023 through 2025 summer seasons designated
approximately 450 candidate hours across the three-summer calibration period, or approximately
150 hours per summer. Those called hours contained all twelve summer coincident-peak
reference intervals for that period. Each fell within hours ending 17 or 18, verified interval by
interval rather than by date alone. The specification, conventions, and known limitations appear
in Appendix A.

The result is stated narrowly because its limits matter as much as its content. The benchmark
does not establish:
       that any customer curtailed load during any candidate hour;
       that any customer's metered demand was reduced or eliminated during any coincident-
       peak interval;
       that any customer avoided any transmission charge;
       that the rule would perform comparably outside its calibration period; or


                                                 1
         that approximately 150 called hours per summer is an acceptable operational burden.
        That depends on load size, opportunity cost, contractual obligations, and whether a call
        requires full or partial reduction. No such estimate is offered here.
What the benchmark does support is narrower and, for this proceeding, more useful. On the
disclosed reference set, the present four-interval methodology was historically reducible to a
finite, reproducible candidate set derived from public information and simple arithmetic. The
Commission should therefore not assume that changing the number or duration of coincident-
peak intervals will by itself eliminate coincident-peak forecasting and strategic load response.
Whether it does so is an empirical question about the structure of monthly peaks, and it can be
answered before adoption rather than discovered after.

B. The benchmark also illustrates what the public record cannot establish.
Public ERCOT data is sufficient to reconstruct the forecast available at the decision time and the
operational system-demand series. Reconstructing the settlement interval ultimately used
requires the authoritative coincident-peak calculation and the adjustments applied to it, including
the treatment of wholesale storage load. Public data is not sufficient to establish what occurred
behind a particular meter, what a customer had committed to do, who held authority to cause that
response, or whether the response satisfied an obligation.
That asymmetry bears directly on this proceeding. The proposed methodology assigns cost
responsibility using measured coincident demand, while the behavior producing that
measurement is governed by contracts, control systems, and operating arrangements outside the
public record. Comments in this docket, including these, are constrained by that limit. So is the
Commission's ability to evaluate the proposal's effects without directing the production of
additional data.

C. Measurement basis: implementation Of the wholesale storage load exclusion.

The proposal excludes wholesale storage load from both DSP 12CP load and ERCOT 12CP
load, defining that term by reference to §25.501(m)(2). The exclusion is clear as drafted. Its
implementation is not.
The Commission should require ERCOT to:

    1. identify, by report and field, the settlement-quality load series and the specific protocol
       calculation that will implement the exclusion;
   2.   clarify the treatment of energy storage charging load that falls outside the defined
        wholesale storage load category; and
   3. publish interval data and workpapers sufficient for distribution service providers and
      affected customer classes to reproduce the resulting twelve-coincident-peak
      determinations independently.
A coincident-peak methodology allocates cost by identifying specific intervals. If reasonable
parties cannot reproduce which intervals were selected, the resulting allocation cannot be audited
by anyone other than the entity that performed it.
This is not a hypothetical concern, and ERCOT has already identified it. In Market Notice M-
B080124-01, ERCOT advised market participants that Real-Time operational Load includes
Wholesale Storage Load while the settlement four-coincident-peak determination excludes it
under Nodal Protocol Section 9.17.1, and advised participants to incorporate the Energy Storage

                                                  2
 Resource charging component if they wished operational monitoring to align with the settlement
calculation. Two series that track each other closely in magnitude can therefore identify different
intervals. A methodology whose selected intervals may affect a twenty-year large-load
minimum-billing obligation should not leave the governing load series to inference.

III. COMMENTS ON PROPOSED §25.193

A. The minimum billing demand, not the number ofcoincident-peak intervals, is the operative
constraint on coincident-peak forecasting.
For large load customers served by investor-owned distribution service providers, proposed
§§25.193(d) and 25.252(e), read together, establish a minimum billing demand equal to the
greater of contracted peak demand, the highest non-coincident peak demand in the preceding
year, or twelve-coincident-peak demand, with billing beginning with the first billing cycle after
transmission capacity is made available and continuing for 240 consecutive monthly payments
across the first twenty years.
Stated precisely: the proposed minimum billing demand cannot be reduced below the contracted-
peak or non-coincident-peak floor through coincident-peak forecasting alone. Other facts can
still change the billed amount, including contract amendment, capacity relinquishment, phased
energization, and changes in actual non-coincident peak demand. But the specific practice of
predicting and avoiding coincident-peak intervals does not reach the floor.
This is worth stating plainly because the move from four intervals to twelve is the more visible
feature of the proposal, while the floor is the provision doing the work.

B. The same provision that limits avoidance also limits the incentive to respond.
Once a large load customer's twelve-coincident-peak demand falls to or below the greater of its
contracted peak demand and its rolling prior-year non-coincident peak, further coincident-peak
reduction no longer reduces its minimum billing demand. A formula that remains in force for
twenty years and is anchored to those measures therefore truncates, rather than eliminates, the
marginal billing incentive for peak response. To the extent the Commission values price-
responsive large load as a reliability resource, the design of that formula and the design of the
coincident-peak methodology are in tension. That tension is a reason to select the formula's
parameters deliberately and on the record, rather than as an incidental consequence of the peak-
counting decision.

C. The record is notyet su/licient to choose among the alternatives the Commission has
identified.
The Commission has asked whether the minimum should vary by customer size or demand,
remain fixed for twenty years, phase down over time, employ a ratchet, employ a weighted
average, or use a lower measure. Each alternative distributes risk differently among the large
load, other customer classes, and the distribution service provider, and the magnitude of those
differences is an empirical question.
The commenter does not recommend a specific alternative, because the available public record
does not support a defensible choice among them. The Commission should instead direct Staff,
ERCOT, and affected distribution service providers to publish sensitivity workpapers
quantifying, under historical conditions, the billing and allocation consequences of at least a
fixed one-hundred-percent floor, a phased or ratcheted floor, a weighted-average floor, and terms

                                                 3
 shorter than twenty years. That record should be made before the Commission adopts a twenty-
year minimum-demand formula anchored to one hundred percent of contracted peak demand or
the rolling prior-year non-coincident peak.

IV. COMMENTS ON PROPOSED §25.252
Proposed §25.252(e)(1) requires billing to begin with the first billing cycle after transmission
capacity is made available. That provision is clear. Three implementation questions surrounding
it are not, and each is consequential enough to warrant express treatment in rule text rather than
being left to tariff, protocol, or contract.
    1.   Determination of availability. The rule should identify the standard for determining the
         date on which transmission capacity is made available, the entity responsible for that
         determination, the notice owed to the customer, and the treatment of partially available
         service.
   2.    Phased energization. Large loads frequently energize in stages over several years, and the
         proposal appears to treat contracted peak demand as a continuing floor. The rule should
         clarify whether contracted peak demand may be defined or amended by an approved
         phased-service schedule and, if so, what documentation, milestones, and effective dates
         govern each phase.
   3.    Capacity relinquishment. The rule should state the effect of relinquishing contracted
         capacity on the minimum billing demand and on the remaining term, and whether that
         capacity becomes available for reallocation under the applicable interconnection process.
Each of these determines the size or duration of an obligation that may run for twenty years and
240 billing cycles. Leaving them to later interpretation invites disputes that express drafting can
prevent.

V. REQUEST FOR DEVELOPMENT OF THE RECORD
The most useful step the Commission can take before adopting a twelve-interval methodology is
to require that the proposed design be tested against historical data and that the results be
published.
The commenter respectfully requests that the Commission direct ERCOT to prepare and publish
a historical backcast of the proposed methodology covering the five annual periods ending
September 30, 2021 through September 30, 2025, that is, October 1, 2020 through September 30,
2025, matching the annual period the proposal itself uses. The backcast should include:

    1. the twelve monthly thirty-minute coincident-peak intervals that would have been selected
       in each annual period under the proposed definitions;
   2. for each month, the selected interval and the next five highest thirty-minute intervals,
      with the megawatt margins separating them, so the Commission can evaluate how
      concentrated, closely contested, and susceptible to displacement the selected intervals
         are;
   3.    a decision-time analysis using archived as-published forecast vintages, so the
         Commission can distinguish how concentrated the monthly peaks were from how
         foreseeable they were to a party acting in advance;



                                                  4
    4. the exact settlement-quality series and averaging method used, identified by report and
      field;
   5. results computed both with and without the proposed wholesale storage load exclusion,
      so the effect of the exclusion is visible;
   6.    distribution service provider and customer class allocation workpapers showing how the
         resulting determinations translate into allocated cost;
    7.   minimum billing demand sensitivities as described in Section III.C; and
   8.    all of the above in machine-readable form sufficient for independent replication.
The interval-selection analysis can be performed from data ERCOT already holds. The allocation
workpapers and minimum-demand sensitivities may require additional tariff, customer-class,
contracted-demand, or billing inputs, and the Commission should direct Staff and affected
distribution service providers to supply them.
These are not open-ended research requests. Each item answers a question the Commission must
otherwise resolve by assumption: how concentrated monthly peaks are compared with summer
peaks; how close the competing intervals are; whether a selected interval is stable against
responsive load; and how allocated cost shifts among classes under actual historical conditions.

VI. CONCLUSION
The commenter takes no position on whether the Commission should adopt a twelve-coincident-
peak methodology. The bounded evidence presented here supports one proposition: on the
disclosed historical reference set, the current four-interval methodology was reducible to a finite
public-data candidate set, in sample, which is a reason to test rather than assume how an
alternative design will behave. Before adoption, the Commission should require a reproducible
historical backcast, candidate-interval margins, an identified measurement basis and storage-
exclusion implementation, and minimum billing demand sensitivities.

 APPENDIX A: BENCHMARK SPECIFICATION AND PROVENANCE

A.1 Decision rule
For each operating day d in a summer month m, the rule designates day d as a candidate day if:

                               Fd k 0.9875 x max( Md, 0.95 x Pm,y-1 )
where:
Fd = the maximum forecast SystemTotal value among the hours ending 16, 17, and 18 on
operating day d, from the in-use model (InUseFlag = Y) in ERCOT report NP3-565-CD, Seven-
Day Load Forecast by Model and Weather Zone, taken from the latest as-published vintage with
a postDatetime at or before 9:00 a.m. Central Prevailing Time on operating day d. Forecast
revisions published after that cutoff are excluded.
Md = the highest daily peak of ERCOT Native Load hourly SystemTotal observed from the first
day of month m through operating day d minus one, using a Central Prevailing Time operating-
day convention. Operating day d is excluded because its afternoon peak has not occurred at the
decision cutoff.

Pm, y-1 = the same-month prior-year reference demand, drawn from the mixed-source reference set
described in A.5.

On a designated candidate day, the rule calls the hours ending 16, 17, and 18 Central Prevailing
Time.

A.2 Conventions
         Vintage selection: the latest as-published vintage with a postDatetime at or before the
         9:00 a.m. cutoff on the operating day. On the historical coincident-peak days in the
         calibration sample this was generally the 8:30 a.m. vintage. Later revisions are excluded.
         Operating day and time convention: dates were assigned using the source's Central-time
         timestamp. The calibration covered June 1 through September 30 only, and every
         calibration date fell within Central Daylight Time, UTC minus five hours, so no daylight
         saving transition occurred within an evaluated window.
         Tie handling: the condition is stated as greater than or equal to, so a value exactly at the
         threshold designates a candidate day.
         Missing data: the calibration implementation treated the absence of an eligible decision-
         time forecast as no call. No operating day in the calibration period lacked an eligible
         forecast, so this convention did not affect the reported result. An operational application
         would require a separately specified missing-data policy.

A.3 Calibration and parameter selection
The threshold was selected by exhaustive search over the values 0.9800 to 1.0000 in increments
of 0.0025. The rule was evaluated on operating days in the 2023,2024, and 2025 summer
seasons. Construction of the prior-year same-month floor also required reference values for 2022
through 2024, so the evaluation period and the input period are not the same. The selection
criterion was to maximize the number of summer coincident-peak reference intervals in the
disclosed calibration set that fell within the called window; among rules achieving maximum
reference-set capture, to minimize total called hours; and to break any remaining tie toward the

                                                   6
 highest threshold value. The selected value is 0.9875, which called all twelve reference intervals
across approximately 450 called hours over the three-summer period.

A.4 Provenance
The final parameterization was frozen on July 3,2026. The dispatch pinning the baseline was
issued July 2,2026. The rule was evaluated on the 2023 through 2025 summer seasons, with
prior-year floor inputs drawn from 2022 through 2024. No 2026 data was used in the calibration
or parameter-selection calculation. The governing evaluation protocol separately discloses the
commenter's prior exposure to certain other June 2026 information.
The rule was not frozen before the beginning of the 2026 summer season. It was frozen before
any July 2026 coincident-peak-plausible day was scored under it.

A.5 Reference data and interval validation
The reference observations used both for scoring and for the prior-year floor are not a single
homogeneous series. ERCOT Native Load files supply the 2022 through 2024 reference
magnitudes and operational monthly-peak dates, which are hourly values. Where corroboration
was available it came from ERCOT-published records of peak demand and from publicly
available reporting. Depending on the observation, those records corroborate the date, the
magnitude, or both. They are not four-coincident-peak settlement determinations. Because the
relevant NP9-83-M records were not retrieved, these observations are not characterized as
primary-sourced settlement determinations. The 2025 values are publicly reported settled fifteen-
minute intervals. ERCOT Native Load includes wholesale storage load; settlement-quality load
excludes it, per ERCOT Nodal Protocols Section 9.17.1 and ERCOT market notice M-B080124-
01. The two quantities agree closely in magnitude and can disagree on which day carries the
monthly peak.
Interval validation was performed rather than assumed. The calibration credits a capture when a
coincident-peak date falls within the called set, and does not itself test the interval. That test was
performed separately for all twelve observations: each reference interval or hourly reference
band falls within hours ending 17 or 18, and imposing the interval-window condition changed no
result. For the 2025 observations the reference timestamps are stored by interval start while the
cited sources describe the intervals by ending time, which accounts for an apparent fifteen-
minute offset. That convention does not resolve the separate June 2025 value discrepancy
between 77,453 MW and 77,490 MW, which is disclosed in Appendix B.

A.6 Limitations ofthe reference data
During preparation of these comments the commenter was unable to retrieve the relevant 2022
through 2024 files of ERCOT's four-coincident-peak calculation product, EMIL NP9-83-M,
through the retrieval method used, and ERCOT's historical four-coincident-peak page publishes
determinations only through 2020. That experience does not establish that the files are
unavailable through every ERCOT channel.

The four 2022 monthly values supply the four 2023 prior-year floors. This limitation is disclosed
rather than resolved, and it is pertinent to Section V: the difficulty of assembling an authoritative,
machine-readable coincident-peak record from public sources is precisely why the Commission
should require ERCOT to publish one.

The decision rule is deterministic arithmetic and uses no proprietary input and no fitted statistical
model. Historical replication is more involved. It requires retrieval and parsing of ERCOT's
archived as-published NP3-565-CD forecast vintages, ERCOT Native Load files, and coincident-
peak determinations subject to the limitations described in A.6, together with the conventions
stated above. The reported result was reproduced from the reference values identified here.
